title: New York Times v. Sullivan
short: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for defamation must prove "actual malice" (knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth); Gertz v. Robert Welch (1974) let states set a lower standard for private figures.
trouble: Students think "actual malice" means ill will toward the person. It is a term of art about the speaker's knowledge of falsity, not about hatred or spite.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Defamation, false statements of fact that harm a person's reputation, was long treated as outside the First Amendment, one of the unprotected categories. In 1964 the Court held that state libel law must still leave room for open debate about public officials.

opts.facts: In 1960 the New York Times ran a full-page advertisement, "Heed Their Rising Voices," supporting the civil rights movement in the South. It contained some factual errors about events in Montgomery, Alabama. L. B. Sullivan, a Montgomery city commissioner over the police, was not named but sued for libel; an Alabama jury awarded him 500,000 dollars.
opts.test: A public official may recover damages for a defamatory falsehood about his official conduct only if he proves "actual malice": that the statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. It must be shown with convincing clarity.
opts.reasoning: Justice Brennan wrote of "a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open." Some false statements are inevitable in free debate; requiring critics to guarantee the truth of every assertion would lead to self-censorship.

blocks.html: The Court then sorted plaintiffs. Public figures, people with general fame or who thrust themselves into a public controversy, must also prove actual malice (Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts, 1967). For private figures, Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) let states choose their own standard, as long as they require at least some fault (usually negligence); but presumed or punitive damages still require actual malice. In Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988) the Court applied the actual malice rule to a claim for emotional distress over a parody that no one could take as fact. Sullivan remains the law. Some justices (Justice Thomas, writing in 2019) have asked whether it should be reconsidered; others defend it as essential to a free press. Both positions appear in the opinions.

blocks.html: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964): a public official suing for defamation must prove actual malice: knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth. Public figures must too; for private figures, Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) lets states set a lower standard, but not liability without fault.

blocks.title: A mayor sues
blocks.q: A newspaper reports that the mayor took a bribe. The report is false; the reporter believed it and checked two sources. Can the mayor win?
steps: The mayor is a public official, and the story concerns official conduct: actual malice is required.
The reporter believed the story and checked sources; there is no knowing falsity or reckless disregard.
Carelessness alone is not actual malice.
blocks.a: No; without actual malice the mayor loses.

blocks.title: A private person
blocks.q: A local blog falsely says a private shop owner sells stolen goods. The blogger did no checking at all, though checking was easy. Under Gertz, what may the state require?
steps: The shop owner is a private figure.
Gertz lets the state set the standard for compensatory damages, as long as it requires fault; negligence is common.
Failing to make easy checks may be negligence. Presumed or punitive damages would need actual malice.
blocks.a: Fault such as negligence for actual damages; actual malice for presumed or punitive damages.

blocks.html: Thinking "actual malice" means ill will toward the person. It is a term of art about the speaker's knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth, not about hatred or spite. A reporter who hates the mayor but believes the story is true, after checking, has no actual malice.
